This chart is about how many countries are full democracies and how long they have maintained that status, grouped into age bands and reported for world regions in 2025.
The source is Our World in Data, and the underlying democracy concept is defined using the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy.

In this framework, a full democracy is a political system where citizens can choose the chief executive and legislature in multi-party, uncertain elections and enjoy freedoms of expression, assembly, and association.
Europe has the largest number of long-standing full democracies, including 15 aged 61-90 years and 11 aged 31-60 years.
North America also has a relatively large stock of older full democracies, with 6 aged 61-90 and 7 aged 31-60.
In the world total for 2025, the largest full-democracy age band is 31-60 years with 35 countries, followed by 61-90 years with 24 countries.
The youngest full-democracy band, aged 1-18, contains 10 countries worldwide, and the 19-30 band contains 8.
Because the definition explicitly includes freedoms of expression, assembly, and association, the chart is relevant not just to election quality but also to broader civic rights.
The chart image and table are not perfectly aligned in scope, because the image presents a world historical series while the table provides regional and world values only for 2025.
